LONDON, England (CNN) — Perhaps it is finally time to resolve the question: should the world’s most popular ball game be known as football or soccer?

Although the issue may appear trivial, the choice between the two names remains one of the sport’s most enduring arguments. At first, the answer seems obvious: FIFA, the game’s international governing organization, includes “football” in its name. But the history is more complicated.

“Soccer” originated in England during the 1880s as an informal abbreviation of “association.” According to the Oxford University Association Football Club’s website, former England captain Charles Wreford-Brown is generally credited with creating the term. It helped distinguish association football from rugby football, which university students called “rugger.”

Despite the widespread assumption that “soccer” is American, the word is therefore British in origin. It is now used most often in nations where “football” can refer to another game. In the United States, for example, the term also describes gridiron football, while Australia has Australian Rules football, an entirely separate sport.

The game was originally called football in the United States as well. The United States of America Football Association was established in 1913. It later became the United States Soccer Football Association and is now called the United States Soccer Federation.

Australia, meanwhile, has an organization named Football Federation Australia. Even so, the national team is unlikely to abandon its “Socceroos” nickname anytime soon—“Footyroos” simply does not have the same ring.

British readers may wonder why the sport’s name is open to debate at all. Yet one of Britain’s most popular television programs is titled “Soccer Saturday,” showing that the distinction is not as straightforward as it might seem.

Even FIFA appears comfortable with both terms. At next year’s FIFA World Cup in South Africa, the gathering place for supporters during the competition will be known as “Soccer City.” Perhaps “football” does not always fit after all.

We want to hear whether you think the sport should be called football or soccer—and your reasons. Share your opinion in the SoundOff box below, take the quick poll on the Football Fanzone homepage, or make a fuller argument by submitting photographs or a video through the Football Fanzone page on iReport.com.

### Football or Soccer?

Few sporting arguments are as persistent as the debate over whether the round-ball game should be called “football” or “soccer.” In much of the world, especially Europe, Africa, Asia, and Latin America, “football” is the ordinary term. In the United States and Canada, however, the sport is generally known as “soccer,” while “football” refers to a different game. Historical evidence shows that neither name is inherently incorrect. Both arose from British sporting traditions, and their modern use largely depends on which code of football became dominant in a particular country.

For much of British history, “football” did not identify a single, standardized sport. It referred broadly to several games in which teams competed over a ball, often under local rules. During the nineteenth century, schools and clubs began formalizing different versions of these games. Two important codes emerged: rugby football, which permitted handling and carrying the ball, and association football, whose rules emphasized kicking and restricted the use of the hands.

The word “soccer” developed as an informal abbreviation of “association football.” In late nineteenth-century England, students—particularly at Oxford—sometimes shortened words and added the suffix “-er.” “Rugby football” became “rugger,” while “association football” was shortened to “assoc.” and eventually became “soccer.” The term was therefore not invented in the United States, as is sometimes claimed. It originated in England and was used by British speakers alongside “football” for many years.

As the various football codes spread around the world, different countries adopted different naming conventions. In places where association football became the leading form of the game, the simple word “football” usually came to mean association football. This is the pattern found in countries such as England, Spain, Germany, Brazil, and Argentina. Local translations—including *fútbol*, *futebol*, and *Fußball*—likewise reflect the sport’s status as the dominant football code.

Elsewhere, another code gained the primary claim to the name “football.” In the United States, American football became the most prominent game bearing that title, so “soccer” remained useful as a clear way to distinguish association football. A similar development occurred in Canada, where Canadian football had an established identity. In Australia, “football” may refer to Australian rules football or rugby league depending on the region, while “soccer” prevents ambiguity. New Zealand, Ireland, and South Africa have also used the two terms in varying proportions because rugby, Gaelic football, or other codes compete for the same linguistic territory.

The names used by organizations reveal the same mixture. The international governing body is FIFA, whose French name translates as the International Federation of Association Football. Many national organizations use “football” in their official titles, even in countries where ordinary speakers often say “soccer.” The United States Soccer Federation is a notable exception, while Australia’s governing body changed its name from Soccer Australia to Football Federation Australia and later to Football Australia. Such choices often reflect efforts to align with international terminology, but they do not necessarily determine everyday speech.

British usage has also changed over time. Although “soccer” was once an accepted British term, “football” gradually became overwhelmingly preferred in Britain. As “soccer” became more closely associated with North American usage, some British speakers began to regard it as foreign or even incorrect. That reaction obscures the word’s British origin. It also shows how language can acquire new cultural associations even when its historical roots remain unchanged.

Ultimately, the dispute is less about correctness than about context. “Football” is the dominant international name and the natural choice in societies where association football holds the strongest claim to the broader term. “Soccer” is equally legitimate, however, and is especially practical in countries where “football” commonly means another sport. The choice between the two words reflects local history, sporting competition, and cultural identity—not a fundamental difference in the game itself.

# It’s football. It’s soccer. And, yes, both are correct

**Opinion**

The world’s most popular sport has 22 players, two goals, one round ball — and an argument over what to call it.

For billions of fans, the answer is obvious: **football**. The game is played primarily with the feet, and that is the name used from Buenos Aires to Barcelona, Lagos to London. FIFA itself is the *Fédération Internationale de Football Association*.

Yet in the United States — as well as in Canada, Australia and several other countries — millions routinely call the sport **soccer**. To some international fans, that sounds like linguistic vandalism, or at least another example of Americans renaming something they did not invent.

There is just one problem with that charge: The word “soccer” came from England.

Modern association football was codified in England in 1863, when the Football Association established rules separating its version of the game from rugby football. In late 19th-century British university slang, students shortened “association” to “assoc.” and added the fashionable “-er” ending. “Assoccer,” and eventually “soccer,” distinguished association football from “rugger,” or rugby football.

In other words, Americans did not create “soccer.” They imported a British term and kept using it after many Britons had moved away from it.

That history gives the pro-soccer camp a strong defense. The word is not incorrect, and in countries with several competing forms of football, it can be helpfully precise. In the United States, “football” generally means the gridiron game of the NFL and college stadiums. In Canada, it may refer to Canadian football. In Australia, “football” can mean Australian rules, rugby league, rugby union or association football, depending on the region and the speaker.

Language follows local custom. Asking Americans to use “football” exclusively for the round-ball game is a little like demanding that Australians agree on a single code whenever someone says “footy.” Context, not international decree, determines meaning.

Still, the case for “football” is overwhelming on the global stage. Variations of the word dominate in most languages: *fútbol* in Spanish, *futebol* in Portuguese, *football* in French and countless local adaptations elsewhere. Even where another native term exists — such as Italian *calcio* — the sport belongs to an international culture that overwhelmingly recognizes it as football.

“Football” also captures the game’s history and emotional reach. It connects neighborhood pitches to the World Cup, local clubs to century-old rivalries. Calling Real Madrid, Liverpool or Boca Juniors “soccer teams” is technically understandable, but to many supporters it sounds as though something has been lost in translation.

There is also a modern irony. Although “soccer” was once used comfortably in Britain — appearing in newspapers, broadcasts and even television program titles — it later became strongly associated with the United States. As that association grew, some British fans began treating the term as foreign or inauthentic. A British word returned home wearing an American accent and was promptly questioned at the border.

But linguistic purity is a poor referee. “Football” itself has never referred to only one perfectly uniform game. For centuries, the term covered a family of sports with different rules, some involving substantial use of the hands. Rugby football, American football, Gaelic football and Australian football all preserve that broader history.

The sensible verdict, then, is not that one side is right and the other ignorant. It is that **“football” is the international default, while “soccer” is a legitimate regional term**.

At a World Cup, in a global headline or in conversation across borders, “football” is usually the most natural and respectful choice. In Dallas, Toronto or Sydney, “soccer” may be clearer. Neither usage changes the game.

And perhaps that should settle the argument. Football’s success has never depended on everyone speaking the same language. Fans cannot even agree on clubs, tactics, referees or the greatest player of all time. Why should the name escape dispute?

Call it football. Call it soccer. Just don’t call it boring.

The whistle blows, the crowd erupts—and somewhere, an argument begins: **Is it football or soccer?**

For most of the world, the answer is simple: football. The sport’s global governing body, **FIFA**—short for *Fédération Internationale de Football Association*—also uses “football” in its official language.

But here’s the twist: **“soccer” originated in Britain.**

In the late 19th century, British students shortened “association football” to “assoc,” then added the fashionable “-er” ending to create “soccer.” The nickname helped distinguish the game from rugby football, sometimes called “rugger.”

Over time, Britain largely settled on “football,” while “soccer” found a lasting home elsewhere. In the **United States**, “football” usually means the gridiron game, so “soccer” remains the standard term. In **Australia**, where Australian rules football and rugby also compete for the football label, both “football” and “soccer” are used. The national governing body is called **Football Australia**, although “soccer” remains widely understood.

Whatever you call it, the game is the same: 11 players, one ball and a sport capable of stopping entire nations in their tracks.

## Your turn: football or soccer?

**Vote:**  
- ⚽ Football  
- ⚽ Soccer  
- ⚽ Either—just play!

# Football or Soccer? It’s the Same Game — and Both Names Belong

Few debates in the sport generate quite as much heat over so little substance. Is it **football**, the name used by most of the world, or **soccer**, the term commonly heard in countries where another code already occupies football’s linguistic territory?

The answer is simple: **both are historically legitimate**. “Football” is the global standard, but “soccer” is not an American corruption. It is a British-born nickname for association football.

## Why it is called association football

In 19th-century Britain, “football” referred to a family of games rather than one universally agreed code. Schools and clubs played under different rules until the Football Association was formed in England in 1863 and began codifying its version.

That game became known as **association football**, distinguishing it from rugby football and other codes. The word “association” was eventually shortened to “assoc,” and, following the Oxford slang habit of adding “-er” to abbreviated words, “assoc” became **“soccer.”**

A similar process turned rugby football into “rugger.”

## Did Charles Wreford-Brown invent “soccer”?

Former England international and influential administrator **Charles Wreford-Brown** is frequently credited with coining the word. According to the popular story, he was asked whether he wanted to play “rugger” and replied that he preferred “soccer.”

Wreford-Brown certainly belonged to the late-Victorian sporting culture from which the term emerged, but the claim that he single-handedly invented it is difficult to prove. Early printed uses show that “soccer” developed as part of a broader slang tradition.

The important point remains: the word originated in Britain, not the United States.

## Why Americans say “soccer”

In the United States, “football” became firmly associated with American football. Calling association football “soccer” therefore provided a useful distinction.

The sport’s governing body also reflects that history. Founded in 1913 as the **United States Football Association**, it later became the United States Soccer Football Association before adopting its current name, the **United States Soccer Federation**, in 1974. Today it is widely branded as **U.S. Soccer**.

That terminology is practical rather than disrespectful. When an American says “soccer,” there is rarely any confusion about which sport is meant. Saying “football” without further explanation can produce exactly the opposite effect.

## “Soccer” is not exclusively American

The United States is far from alone. Countries with strong rival football codes have often used “soccer” to distinguish the round-ball game from Australian rules, rugby league, rugby union or gridiron.

Australia’s men’s national team offer the most famous example: the **Socceroos**. The nickname, combining “soccer” and “kangaroos,” has survived even though the country’s governing body changed its name from Soccer Australia to Football Federation Australia—and later to Football Australia.

Britain itself has never completely abandoned the word either. **Soccer Saturday**, the long-running Sky Sports programme, has used it prominently in the home of the Premier League. Nobody watching assumes the show is about the NFL.

South Africa provides another reminder. Johannesburg’s FNB Stadium is widely known as **Soccer City**, the venue that hosted the opening match and final of the 2010 FIFA World Cup. “Soccer” there coexists comfortably with “football,” especially in a country where rugby has its own enormous cultural presence.

## Why “football” still wins globally

Although both terms are valid, **football** is unquestionably the international default. FIFA’s name comes from the French *Fédération Internationale de Football Association*, clubs from Liverpool to Boca Juniors use football in their identities, and supporters across Europe, Africa, Asia and South America overwhelmingly speak of football.

The name also feels natural: the game is primarily played with the feet and a ball. In most football cultures, “soccer” can sound foreign, old-fashioned or overly commercial.

That preference deserves respect—but it does not turn “soccer” into an incorrect word.

## The final verdict

Call it **football** when speaking globally or in a country where that is the established term. Call it **soccer** where doing so distinguishes it from another kind of football. Adapt to your audience, and everyone will know what game you mean.

The terminology debate is not really about right and wrong. It is about geography, history and local sporting culture.

Football is the world’s preferred name. Soccer is its authentic British nickname. Both point to the same beautiful game—and there are far better things for supporters to argue about, starting with the referee’s last decision.

## Soccer? It’s More British Than You Think

Mention the word *soccer* in an English pub and somebody will inevitably splutter into their pint: “It’s called football!”

Fair enough—but blaming the Americans for inventing *soccer* is rather like blaming them for inventing tea. The word actually emerged in late-19th-century England, when school and university slang had a habit of shortening words and adding “-er”. Rugby football became *rugger*; Association Football—named after the Football Association—was clipped from “association” to *assoc*, and then turned into *soccer*.

The term is often linked with former England international Charles Wreford-Brown, an Oxford-educated administrator who helped shape the early game. In other words, *soccer* did not arrive wearing a baseball cap and clutching a hot dog. It came with an English accent.

So why do Americans use it? Because they already have another sport called football: the gridiron game of helmets, quarterbacks and tactical pauses long enough to repaint the kitchen. Saying *soccer* avoids confusion.

The same logic applies in Australia, where “football” may mean Australian rules, rugby league or rugby union depending on where you are and whom you ask. Association football therefore becomes *soccer* in everyday conversation—even though the national governing body now officially calls the sport football.

England is different because Association Football became the country’s dominant code. Here, *football* needs no explanation, while *soccer* can sound imported despite its thoroughly British birth certificate.

That is the real pattern: countries with several competing football codes tend to use *soccer* for clarity. Countries where Association Football reigns supreme usually just call it *football*.

So, no need for linguistic extra time or a penalty shoot-out: both names are historically legitimate. But which side are you on—**football or soccer?**
